## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet, and the starting network scored 0/0. So there is no evidence yet, and seed noise could account for any small difference. I see two likely causes of the zero score. (1) The budget is tiny: 131k steps, about 32 updates with the default recipe, which may be too few for PPO to learn exact multi-brick builds. Fewer PPO epochs give more samples and more updates. (2) Perception: to score a placement correctly, the network must find the landing layer (the highest build height under the footprint) and check that the target fills that layer across the footprint without leaving missing cells beneath. Pooled 2D column features make this joint test hard. A layer-wise view (per-layer features, pooled over footprints, then merged across layers) makes it close to linear. Round 1 is a factorial: the recipe alone (A), the layer-wise network with the same recipe (B), and the layer-wise network with one PPO epoch for more samples (C).

### Round 2
All four runs so far score exactly 0, on dev and in training (train success over the last 10% is also 0). That covers the default recipe, a sample-rich recipe, a layer-relative network built to make landing logic easy, and 1 vs 2 PPO epochs. Since the network built for landing logic also failed, perception is probably not the only bottleneck. All round-1 runs used low entropy (0.003) with lr 2e-3, and the default (entropy 0.01) also failed. Early on, most random placements put cells outside the target and lose reward, while DONE pays 0. So I suspect PPO locks in early to DONE or to a narrow policy before it finds placements that fill only target cells. This round tests that with a high-entropy, longer-horizon recipe (entropy 0.03, gamma 0.98, lambda 0.95, lr 7e-4, 3 epochs) on the starting net and on the layer net, so the two differ only in architecture. The third candidate adds a separate critic, the mask as input, and a 3x3 per-type output, in case actions are anchored differently than described.

### Round 3
All six trials score exactly 0, both on dev and in training (train_success_last10pct = 0). This holds across two architectures, recipes with high and low entropy, 1 to 3 epochs, and up to 338k steps. Designs with 6 drops should give at least a few percent if the agent learned anything, so this looks like a systematic mismatch rather than seed noise or too little training. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. A 3x3 output conv (r2c3) would have absorbed small anchor offsets, and that also scored 0. The remaining suspects are an action indexing that local per-cell conv heads cannot express: transposed y/x, a different anchor convention, reordered brick types, or DONE at a different index. A fully connected action head can learn any fixed mapping, so this round tests that: a conv trunk with an added FC head under two recipes, and a pure MLP that assumes no layout.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored 0 on dev and had 0 training success. That covers the starting net, the layer scorer, the conv+FC hybrid and a plain MLP, each with low-entropy, high-entropy, 1-epoch and slow recipes. Changing the recipe alone did not move the score, and nothing has shown a signal above noise. My best guess is that greedy exact builds need precise per-placement checks that the current heads cannot compute well. To place a brick correctly, the net must find the footprint's landing layer, the maximum column height under the footprint. Then it must check, for every footprint cell, that the target has a cell at that layer and no empty target gap below it. Pooling min, max and mean over the footprint, as the PoolHead does, cannot express this two-stage dependency. In this last round I test a head that does the two stages explicitly: pool learned landing features over the footprint, then judge each footprint cell with a shared MLP and pool the judgements. The three candidates use different recipes and inputs.
